article:
A name is not a website

A domain is a sticker. DNS is the instruction that says where the sticker leads. Buying bohobond.com does nothing until a record points at the host. This is where most beginners freeze, because the words look like a priesthood and the change takes minutes that feel like days.

You buy the name from a registrar. You point it at Vercel, or wherever the site lives. You wait. You try www and the bare name. You do not refresh every three seconds like it owes you an apology.

The records you will actually meet

A record: this name goes to this address. CNAME: this name is an alias for that other name. TXT: a note used to prove you own the thing — email, certificates, sometimes a random check. Nameservers: who is in charge of the instructions. If you change nameservers, you are moving the whole filing cabinet.

TTL is how long the old instruction is allowed to linger. Patience is part of DNS. So is writing down what you changed.

How I actually do it

Each product gets a name when it is real enough to say out loud. sendreorder.com. scratchbox.xyz. bohobond.com. I add the domain in Vercel and copy what it asks for. I do not invent records. When apex and www disagree, I fix that before I redesign anything.

Open Mailer will force this chapter to get sharper: one mailbox, many domains. That is DNS as a product, not as homework.

Where noobs get stuck

Buying five names and shipping zero. Pointing the domain at the old host. Forgetting www. Or moving nameservers “because a tutorial said so” and breaking email at the same time.

Film this

Buy nothing live on camera if you do not want to. Show the Vercel domain screen and the registrar DNS screen side by side. Draw an arrow. Then load the name on a phone that is not on your wifi.

Do this before chapter 08

  • Pick one name. One.
  • Point it at the production host. Follow the host’s own docs, not a 2019 gist.
  • Check apex and www.
  • Do not touch email records until the next chapters say so.
